note: Subjects/9702 Physics/09 Electricity/9.2 Potential difference and power.md
outline: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge: $V=W/Q$, with $1\,\mathrm{V}=1\,\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$. Electrical power is energy transferred per second. Combining $W=VQ$ with $I=Q/t$ gives $P=VI$. For a resistor obeying $V=IR$, substitute to obtain $P=I^2R$ or $P=V^2/R$. At fixed resistance power scales with the square of current or voltage.

misconceptions.statement: Defining potential difference as energy transferred by a unit charge, without a ratio.
misconceptions.refutation: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, a ratio W/Q.
misconceptions.contrast: 10 J transferred by 2 C gives 5 V, not 10 J.

misconceptions.statement: Confusing energy per charge with energy per current.
misconceptions.refutation: Charge, measured in coulombs, is the denominator in V=W/Q.

misconceptions.statement: Assuming power always varies linearly with current or voltage for fixed resistance.
misconceptions.refutation: At fixed R, P=I²R=V²/R, so doubling current or voltage quadruples power.
misconceptions.contrast: A 50% increase in power makes current √1.5 times as large, not 1.5 times.

misconceptions.statement: Using P=V²/R without checking whether compared components share the same voltage.
misconceptions.refutation: In series the current is common; use P=I²R. In parallel the voltage is common; use P=V²/R.
misconceptions.contrast: Two series resistors R and 2R dissipate powers in the ratio 1:2.

misconceptions.statement: Equal current throughout a series circuit means its current cannot change when the circuit changes.
misconceptions.refutation: At a given instant, series components carry equal current; after the total resistance changes, recalculate current using the supply p.d. and new total resistance.
misconceptions.contrast: A fixed 12 V supply gives 1 A at total resistance 12 ohms and 0.5 A at 24 ohms, with equal current at all series positions in each state.
misconceptions.source: https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/567861-june-2024-examiner-report.pdf (9702/22, Q5(b)); bundle ER 9702 w22 P22 Q6 and s22 P21 Q6

items.examiner: Many candidates found this question difficult, selecting A rather than B. In the question, point P is at a higher potential than point Q (as indicated by the + and – signs). This means that work needs to be done to move a positive charge from Q to P (the positive charge is repelled by point P so has to be ‘pushed’ towards it). As 1 V is 1 J C–1, the energy needed to transfer +1 C from Q to P is 1 J.

Point A is at a potential of $4\ \mathrm{V}$ and point B is at $5\ \mathrm{V}$. A charge of $+1\ \mathrm{C}$ is moved between them without changing its kinetic energy; ignore friction. Determine which direction, A to B or B to A, requires positive work supplied by an external agent, and how much work is required. Give a reason for your choice.

rubric.point: The direction is A to B.
Moving positive charge to higher potential increases its electric potential energy.

items.explanation: A to B moves positive charge to higher potential, increasing its electric potential energy, so an external agent must supply work. With no change in kinetic energy, $W=Q(V_B-V_A)=(1)(5-4)=1\ \mathrm{J}$. In the reverse direction the electric potential energy decreases.
hints: Consider whether the energy of the positive charge rises or falls in each direction.
Relate work supplied to the change in electric potential energy when kinetic energy is unchanged.
Use the potential at the destination minus the potential at the starting point in $W=Q\Delta V$.

9702-9.2.1.motivate: A lamp transfers electrical energy into light and thermal energy. Voltage tells us how much is transferred for each coulomb that passes through it.
9702-9.2.1.establish: Define the potential difference across a component as the energy transferred per unit charge. The word *per* states a ratio: $V=W/Q$. Energy is in joules, charge in coulombs, so $1\ \mathrm{V}=1\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$. A p.d. of $5\ \mathrm{V}$ means $5\ \mathrm{J}$ is transferred for each coulomb through that component.
9702-9.2.1.connect: Charge is the quantity moved through the component; the energy transfer depends on both that charge and the p.d. across it.
9702-9.2.1.note:
- Potential difference across a component is energy transferred per unit charge.
- $V=W/Q$ and $1\ \mathrm{V}=1\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$.
9702-9.2.1.self_explain: Why is ‘energy transferred per unit charge’ more precise than ‘energy transferred by a unit charge’?
9702-9.2.1.plain_words: Potential difference compares energy transfer with the amount of charge passing through a named component. More joules for each coulomb means a larger voltage; it does not by itself tell you how much charge passes each second.

forms.example: Stage 1: A lamp transfers $18\ \mathrm{J}$ when $3.0\ \mathrm{C}$ passes. Identify energy and charge for this same lamp. Stage 2: $V=W/Q=18/3.0=6.0\ \mathrm{V}$. Stage 3: This means $6.0\ \mathrm{J}$ transferred per coulomb, not an energy of six joules independent of charge. To measure it, connect one voltmeter terminal to each side of the lamp, in parallel. The meter compares the potentials of those two points.

misconceptions.fix: Say energy transferred per unit charge; divide joules by coulombs to obtain volts.

9702-9.2.2.motivate: Knowing the energy transferred and charge passing through a component lets you calculate its p.d. directly.
9702-9.2.2.establish: Recall and use $V=W/Q$. Here $V$ is the p.d. across the component, $W$ is energy transferred across it and $Q$ is the charge passing through it. Rearrange to $W=VQ$ or $Q=W/V$ when another quantity is unknown. For $24\ \mathrm{J}$ transferred by $6.0\ \mathrm{C}$, $V=24/6.0=4.0\ \mathrm{V}$.
9702-9.2.2.connect: The equation is the mathematical form of the definition of potential difference; current can supply charge via $Q=It$.
9702-9.2.2.note:
- $V=W/Q$; use joules and coulombs.
- Rearrange to $W=VQ$ or $Q=W/V$.
9702-9.2.2.self_explain: A component transfers $18\ \mathrm{J}$ at $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$. How much charge passes through it?
9702-9.2.2.plain_words: First distinguish the charge that passes from its rate of flow. For constant current, multiply current by elapsed time to obtain charge. Then multiply that charge by the p.d. across the same component to obtain the energy it transfers.

forms.example: Stage 1: A component has constant p.d. $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and current $40\ \mathrm{mA}$ for $2.0\ \mathrm{min}$. Convert: $I=0.040\ \mathrm{A}$ and $t=120\ \mathrm{s}$. Stage 2: $Q=It=0.040\times120=4.8\ \mathrm{C}$. Stage 3: $W=VQ=6.0\times4.8=28.8\ \mathrm{J}$, or $29\ \mathrm{J}$ to two significant figures. The current is a rate, so it cannot replace charge in $W=VQ$.

misconceptions.temptation: The current is often supplied in the question, so it seems natural to put it in the denominator.
misconceptions.fix: Current is charge per second: obtain Q = It first, then use V = W/Q; energy divided by current alone is not voltage.

9702-9.2.2.diagram_reason: This form concerns a sequence of scalar calculations; explicit unit conversions and equations show the reasoning without a circuit drawing.
source_gaps: The reviewed textbook pages establish W = VQ but do not supply this combined current-time form; Q = It comes from the bundled prerequisite and the example and check are original applications.

9702-9.2.3.motivate: Two devices at the same voltage can transfer energy at different rates. Power measures that rate.
9702-9.2.3.establish: Recall and use $P=VI$ for electrical power. From $P=W/t$, $W=VQ$ and $I=Q/t$, it follows that $P=VI$. For a resistor obeying $V=IR$, substitute to obtain $P=I^2R$ and $P=V^2/R$. Choose the equation matching the known quantities. For a fixed resistance, doubling current or p.d. makes power four times as large, because it is proportional to their squares. The p.d. and current must refer to the component whose power you calculate.
9702-9.2.3.connect: This combines energy per charge with charge per second: energy per second is power. Ohm's law gives the two resistor forms.
9702-9.2.3.note:
- Electrical power: $P=VI$, measured in watts.
- For a resistor: $P=I^2R=V^2/R$.
- At fixed $R$, power varies with the square of current or p.d.
9702-9.2.3.self_explain: Why does increasing the current in a fixed resistor by $50\%$ increase power by more than $50\%$?
9702-9.2.3.plain_words: Power is energy transferred each second. Multiply energy per coulomb by coulombs per second to get power. When comparing resistors, establish whether they share current or share potential difference before choosing a power formula.

forms.name: Derive and use electrical power
wordings: Show that P = VI from the definitions of p.d., current and power.
Calculate the power of a named component.
forms.example: Stage 1: Write $V=W/Q$, $I=Q/t$ and $P=W/t$. Stage 2: For constant p.d. and current, substitute $W=VQ$: $P=VQ/t=V(Q/t)=VI$. Stage 3: A component transfers $12\ \mathrm{J}$ while $6.0\ \mathrm{C}$ passes in $3.0\ \mathrm{s}$. Its own $V=12/6.0=2.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and $I=6.0/3.0=2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ give $P=4.0\ \mathrm{W}$, checked by $12/3.0=4.0\ \mathrm{W}$. Use the voltage across and the current through this component, not a supply value belonging elsewhere.
forms.check: A heater operates at a constant $12\ \mathrm{V}$ and $0.50\ \mathrm{A}$. How long does it take to transfer $180\ \mathrm{J}$?

rubric.point: Finds the time as 30 s by any valid method, including using 6.0 W or W = VIt.

forms.name: Compare resistor power using the shared quantity
wordings: Compare powers of resistors in series and in parallel.
Explain what must remain fixed for a stated power proportionality.
forms.example: Stage 1: For $4.0\ \Omega$ and $8.0\ \Omega$ in series carrying $0.50\ \mathrm{A}$, identify shared current. $P=I^2R$ gives $1.0\ \mathrm{W}$ and $2.0\ \mathrm{W}$. Stage 2: Put them in parallel with $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ across each: $P=V^2/R$ gives $9.0\ \mathrm{W}$ and $4.5\ \mathrm{W}$. Thus larger resistance means larger power only when current is held fixed, and smaller power when p.d. is held fixed. Stage 3: For a single fixed resistor, multiplying its p.d. by $1.5$ multiplies its power by $1.5^2=2.25$. Stage 4: Equal series current refers to all positions at one instant. With an ideal constant $12\ \mathrm{V}$ supply, increasing total series resistance from $12\ \Omega$ to $24\ \Omega$ reduces current from $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ to $0.50\ \mathrm{A}$.
forms.check: Two fixed resistors, A of $10\ \Omega$ and B of $30\ \Omega$, first carry $0.20\ \mathrm{A}$ in series. Calculate each power and justify the comparison. They are then connected in parallel with $12\ \mathrm{V}$ across each: calculate their powers and explain the reversal. Separately, state the power factor when the p.d. across one fixed resistor is multiplied by $1.8$. Finally, a series circuit on an ideal constant $12\ \mathrm{V}$ supply has its total resistance increased from $40\ \Omega$ to $60\ \Omega$; calculate the current before and after, and explain why equal series current does not imply unchanged current.
forms.answer: Series: shared $I$ gives $P_A=0.20^2\times10=0.40\ \mathrm{W}$ and $P_B=1.2\ \mathrm{W}$; at the same current $P\propto R$. Parallel: shared $V$ gives $P_A=144/10=14.4\ \mathrm{W}$ and $P_B=144/30=4.8\ \mathrm{W}$; at the same p.d. $P\propto1/R$. Multiplying p.d. by $1.8$ multiplies power by $1.8^2=3.24$ for the fixed resistor. For the separate circuit, $I=12/40=0.30\ \mathrm{A}$ initially and $12/60=0.20\ \mathrm{A}$ finally. Current is equal at all series positions in each state, but the changed total resistance changes its value.
forms.source: https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/567861-june-2024-examiner-report.pdf (9702/22, Q5(b)); bundle ER 9702 w22 P22 Q6 and s22 P21 Q6

rubric.point: Identifies the shared series current and obtains 0.40 W and 1.2 W for A and B respectively by any valid method, including P = VI with Ohm’s law.
Identifies the shared parallel potential difference and obtains 14.4 W and 4.8 W for A and B respectively by any valid method, including P = VI with Ohm’s law.
Explains power increases with resistance at fixed current but decreases with resistance at fixed p.d.
Gives a power factor of 3.24, accepting equivalent calculations; the supplied fixed resistance need not be repeated.
Finds currents 0.30 A and 0.20 A using the total resistance and the fixed supply p.d.
Distinguishes equal current along a series circuit at an instant from a current that changes between circuit states.

misconceptions.idea: At fixed resistance, power changes in direct proportion to current or p.d.
misconceptions.temptation: P = VI looks linear if the other factor is silently treated as constant.
misconceptions.fix: At fixed resistance V changes with I; use the squared ratio in P = I squared R or P = V squared divided by R.

misconceptions.idea: Power is always inversely proportional to resistance, even when resistors are in series.
misconceptions.temptation: P = V squared divided by R seems to settle every comparison.
misconceptions.fix: First identify the shared quantity: series shares current; parallel across the same two nodes shares p.d.

misconceptions.idea: Equal current throughout a series circuit means its current cannot change when the circuit changes.
misconceptions.temptation: The phrase same current is taken to mean unchanged over time.
misconceptions.fix: At a given instant, series components carry equal current; after the total resistance changes, recalculate current using the supply p.d. and new total resistance.
